"""
The emergence of organized spatiotemporal patterns is a hallmark of oscillatory systems, from neural populations to engineered networks. Detecting and tracking these patterns is particularly challenging when systems exhibit transient dynamics. In this work, we introduce a framework based on spatial ordinal patterns to characterize the spatiotemporal dynamics of oscillatory systems. Our method operates directly on phase information, rather than amplitude, and incorporates additional patterns to account for nearly equal phases. This symbolic representation encodes local spatial ordering, capturing both phase gradients and synchronized clusters within a unified approach. Using this representation, we define a spatial permutation entropy that quantifies the diversity of spatiotemporal patterns at each time point, enabling real-time detection of transient dynamics and regime transitions. We demonstrate that this approach distinguishes phase-locked states with identical global synchronization but different spatial organizations, and also characterizes partially synchronized states. We validate the method on synthetic oscillator networks across diverse spatiotemporal regimes, as well as on resting-state EEG recordings from human volunteers, where it differentiates between conditions within individual subjects.
